title: Inheritance: Constructors, Access Control, and Types
relevance: SDE interviews use inheritance to probe whether candidates grasp object lifetime order, access boundaries, and diamond/virtual-inheritance layout—not just the is-a relationship.

phases.goal: Establish construction/destruction order, the protected access level, and the standard inheritance graph shapes.

must_hit.point: On construction the base-class constructor runs first, then the derived-class constructor.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says base is built before derived / construction proceeds from the base outwards.

must_hit.point: On destruction the order reverses: derived destructor runs first, then the base destructor.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says most-derived tears down first, then base cleans up the foundation.

must_hit.point: A protected member is inaccessible through an object from outside, but accessible inside derived classes (unlike private, which derived classes cannot access).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts private vs protected for derived access and notes outsiders cannot use obj.member on protected.

must_hit.point: Inheritance shapes include single, multilevel, hierarchical, multiple, and hybrid combinations.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names several of: one base, chain A→B→C, many from one base, one from many bases, or mixed graphs.

probes: Walk through what prints when a Derived object that publicly inherits Base is created and then destroyed.
What does protected buy you that private and public do not, and who can access it?

hints.1: Think about which part of the object must exist before the specialised part can run.
hints.2: Construction goes base→derived; destruction is the reverse; then contrast private/protected/public for derived vs outside.
hints.3: Base ctor first, derived ctor second; derived dtor first, base dtor second; protected acts private externally but is usable in derived classes.

phases.goal: Show how base constructors are invoked from derived classes and how the diamond problem arises and is fixed with virtual inheritance.

must_hit.point: By default a derived object invokes the base’s no-argument constructor; to pass arguments to a parameterised base constructor you must call it from the derived member-initialiser list.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions default/no-arg base ctor and initialiser-list syntax like Entity(playerName) before the body.

must_hit.point: You cannot initialise base-class members directly in the derived constructor body or initialiser list; you must delegate to the base constructor.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Rejects e.g. initialising name in Player’s list and says call the Entity/base constructor instead.

must_hit.point: When a graph splits and merges (diamond), non-virtual multiple inheritance from a common base creates a distinct base subobject per path, causing name-lookup ambiguity and duplicated base-member footprint.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explains two Person copies and why ta.age is ambiguous without qualification/virtual inheritance.

must_hit.point: Virtual inheritance (e.g. class B : virtual public A) makes intermediates share a single common-base subobject, typically reached via hidden pointers or offsets rather than embedding a duplicate in each path.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says Teacher/Student use virtual public Person so TeachingAssistant has one shared Person.

probes: If Entity only has Entity(std::string), how must Player’s constructor start Entity?
What goes wrong with ta.age in a Teacher/Student/Person diamond without virtual inheritance, and how does virtual inheritance change the layout?

hints.1: Base subobjects are not free-form fields you assign in the derived ctor.
hints.2: Use the member-initialiser list to call the base ctor; for diamonds, count how many Person subobjects exist on each path.
hints.3: Player(...) : Entity(playerName), score(...); without virtual, two Person subobjects make age ambiguous; virtual public shares one Person via hidden offsets/pointers.

phases.goal: Weigh multiple inheritance’s power against complexity, and virtual inheritance’s sharing against layout/creation cost.

must_hit.point: Multiple inheritance is powerful but adds significant structural complexity (and leads into challenges like the diamond problem).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Acknowledges MI capability while warning about graph complexity / diamond fallout.

must_hit.point: Virtual inheritance avoids duplicating the common base but makes object creation slightly slower and memory layouts heavier, which is why it is opt-in.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States sharing wins on duplication, with slower creation and heavier layouts as the cost of opting in.

probes: When would you choose virtual inheritance over plain multiple inheritance from a shared base?
What costs make virtual inheritance opt-in rather than the default?

hints.1: Duplication and ambiguity are the failure mode; sharing is the fix with a price.
hints.2: Compare duplicated base subobjects vs one shared subobject at the end of the most-derived object.
hints.3: Use virtual inheritance when paths would otherwise duplicate a common base; accept slightly slower creation and heavier layouts because sharing is not free.

phases.goal: Apply the diamond-problem story and virtual-inheritance fix the way an interviewer expects it answered.

must_hit.point: A classic answer names the diamond problem as duplicated base subobjects with ambiguous access, resolved in C++ by virtual inheritance so intermediates share a single base instance.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States ambiguity of duplicated bases and immediately cites class B : virtual public A / shared instance via hidden offsets.

must_hit.point: The TeachingAssistant inheriting Teacher and Student, both from Person, is the concrete diamond scenario: without virtual inheritance age is ambiguous; with virtual public on the intermediates, a single Person exists and age can be set.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Retells Person/Teacher/Student/TeachingAssistant and contrasts ambiguous age vs OK after virtual inheritance.

probes: What is the diamond problem and how is it resolved in C++?
Sketch a TeachingAssistant that is both Teacher and Student under a shared Person—what breaks and what do you change?

hints.1: Draw the inheritance graph that splits then merges.
hints.2: Ambiguity comes from two base subobjects; the language fix is on the intermediate inherits.
hints.3: Say duplicated Person subobjects make ta.age ambiguous; fix with Teacher/Student as virtual public Person so one Person is shared.

tradeoffs.topic: Plain multiple inheritance vs virtual inheritance
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Plain MI from a common non-virtual base keeps a distinct base subobject per path (simple embedding, but duplication and ambiguity). Virtual inheritance shares one base subobject via hidden pointers/offsets, preventing duplication at the cost of slightly slower creation and heavier layouts—so it is opt-in.

tradeoffs.topic: Multiple inheritance power vs structural complexity
tradeoffs.strong_answer: MI lets one type combine several bases (e.g. SmartPhone from Phone and Camera) but introduces complex graphs that readily produce diamond duplication and harder reasoning about layout and name lookup.

gotchas.trap: Writing something like Player() : name("Bob") {} to set a base member from the derived initialiser list or body.
gotchas.correction: Base members are not directly initialisable there; call the base constructor from the derived member-initialiser list and let it initialise its own members.

gotchas.trap: Assuming ta.age works in a Teacher/Student/Person diamond without virtual inheritance.
gotchas.correction: Each path carries its own Person subobject, so age is an ambiguous name lookup until intermediates use virtual inheritance to share one Person.

gotchas.trap: Expecting destruction to follow the same order as construction.
gotchas.correction: Destruction is exactly reversed: derived destructor first, then base.

gotchas.trap: Treating protected like public for outside code via obj.member.
gotchas.correction: Protected is not accessible through an object from outside; only the defining class and derived classes may use it, while public remains the only level usable as obj.member from anywhere.
